recognition.text: NASA Webb image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Thousands of overlapping objects fill this black field, from members of a massive galaxy cluster to distorted galaxies far behind it. The biggest bright white oval, a supergiant elliptical galaxy, is the dominant member of MACS J1423, a cluster about 5 billion light-years away in the constellation Boötes. Webb's NIRCam took the image in 2023.

The cluster's gravity works as a lens, magnifying and distorting light from objects well behind it. This gravitational lensing lets astronomers study distant galaxies in detail. One of them is the Firefly Sparkle, a galaxy seen as it was around 600 million years after the big bang. Stretched into a long arc, it shows 10 distinct star clusters that give off most of its light.

The Firefly Sparkle has a mass similar to what the Milky Way's might have been at the same early stage. Its clusters formed at different times, and its stars have not settled into a central bulge or a thin disk, signs that the galaxy is still assembling. Two companion galaxies sit close by and may shape how it grows.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam took this near-infrared image. NASA shows F115W and F150W in blue, F200W and F277W in green, and F356W and F444W in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colors here are hues assigned to Webb filters.

explore: Webb surveyed the same field that Hubble imaged for its CLASH program, which used Wide Field Camera 3, and its near-infrared sharpness revealed many more galaxies in far greater detail. The observation is part of the CAnadian NIRISS Unbiased Cluster Survey (CANUCS). The Firefly Sparkle sits 6,500 light-years from its first companion and 42,000 light-years from its second.
